description: From 1st grader to Stanford college student, our team is dedicated for school-age space fans, Mini Bot turns 187,000 kg of lunar hardware and 7,000 kg of Martian hardware into short, funny, and touching games online and offline— about the science they did, why they were left behind, and why they still matter.
summary:
Space Relics answers the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge by turning NASA's discarded equipment into game and board games online and offline that children can play. For kids, families, and community groups, it covers relics on the Moon, Mars, deep space, from the Apollo 11 "Eagle" lander to the Ingenuity helicopter.
After the challenge, we'll partner with AIRII and nonprofits like the California Academy of Sciences and the Tech interactive to demo the game, card deck, 3D-printed figures and rovers, and our online interactive games at Bay Area libraries, schools, and events, as ambassadors.
details:
Purpose and audience

Space Relics is an educational game for school-age children, families and community groups who are curious about space. It introduces NASA equipment left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space after its mission ended. Every relic in the game is tied to its mission, what it added to NASA science, and how it came to rest where it is.

We want children to see that this equipment still matters. It marks the places where people first reached other worlds, and some of it, like the laser reflectors left by Apollo astronauts, is still used by scientists today.

Offline and online versions

The offline version is a printed board game with cards and a Field Manual of rules. It needs no screen, is quick to learn, and works for classrooms, community events and family game nights.

Beyond the challenge, our team will work with AIRII and other nonprofits such as the California Academy of Sciences to bring Space Relics to the communities around us. We will demo the board game, our deck of cards, and the 3D-printed figures and rovers at libraries, schools, and community events across the Bay Area, so children and families can play the game, hold the models in their hands, and hear the stories of the machines left on the Moon and Mars. Our team members will be ambassadors to the local public — sharing what we learned, teaching others to play, and inviting more kids to join the next expedition.

The online version opens from one Launch Pad link with two doors:

  • Exploration ("Discovering the Explorers Left Behind"): players drive SCOUT, a rover, on missions to the Moon and Mars. They visit equipment left behind, such as Surveyor 3 and Sojourner, and learn what really happened to it after its mission ended.
  • Expedition: the board game on screen, played competitively or in co-op mode. It saves progress, so players can pick up where they left off.

The heart of the online version is the Relic Passport, which joins both games in one loop: Explore it, Restore it, Stamp it. Players find a relic in Exploration, restore its site by building stations in Expedition, and collect a stamp for each one. Collecting stamps gives children a reason to come back, and we will keep polishing and updating the online version so there is always more to discover.

Gameplay and learning

Players join the Relic Recovery Corps, a team of young astronauts in the year 2069, a century after the first Moon landing. They fly a loop from Earth Base to the Moon, across to Mars and out to deep space, stopping at relics along the way. The Corps Code sets the tone: leave the footprints, say the names of the people behind each mission, and share what you learn.

Each turn has three steps: Launch (roll the dice and move), Explore (do what the tile says) and Build (grow one site you lead). On an unopened relic, a player reads its Dossier card aloud and can spend Supply Pods to open a site. They become its Site Lead, but the relic belongs to everyone.

Every site grows through four stations, and each one answers a question about the relic:

  1. Beacon: What is it?
  2. Survey Camp: How did it come to rest here?
  3. Dig Station: Who made it happen?
  4. Heritage Station: What did it teach us?

Supply Pods are scarce, so knowledge is the real fuel. Landing on a friend's site starts a Knowledge Exchange: answer its Field Question correctly, and you take a Pod while their site grows. Players can also Call for Help, or share a fun fact at their own site in Show & Tell. Signal cards based on real missions, such as LCROSS and GRAIL, move players or send help. From the second game on, players pick Crew Roles inspired by real astronauts, such as a Geologist inspired by Harrison Schmitt.

The game contains multiple modes with different objective to improve re-playability and accommodate for various style of groups and parties, typically in a default setup, the objective is to get enough Heritage Stations completed to open the Launch Window. Before scoring, each player tells the story of their favorite relic in one sentence. The player with the most markers becomes Chief Archivist, and every restored story belongs to the whole team. Families can also play Storm Season, a co-op mode where everyone races a dust storm together.

Learning is built into the rules. Players read every card aloud, answer questions, and teach each other so friends can help them later. A Detective's Notebook asks players to guess why each relic went quiet, such as power running out or dust covering its solar panels, before reading the answer. After each game, grown-ups ask "Why did you choose that?" to talk through strategy.

In Exploration, players drive SCOUT and inspect real equipment on the Moon and Mars. Every fact is labeled as real mission history or as a made-up part of the game, so children always know which is which.

Challenge considerations

What age group is the story designed for? School-age children, playing with their family, classmates or community group. The rules are built for mixed ages: a grown-up can read cards aloud, younger players can get a hint or choose between two answers instead of three, and a First Expedition mode leaves out the advanced rules for a first game. Luckily our team consist several targeted age kids to play, their feedback gets us improving round by round. 

How accessible is the format? The board game is printable, needs no screen or internet, and sets up in about five minutes. Every card is read aloud, so children who are still learning to read can join in. The online version runs in a web browser with nothing to install, and it saves progress so players can come back later.

Through the local NPOs our team works with, students who are interested in STEM will have a chance to get their hands on the game and play on-site. Our physical deck of cards of the equipments will also be passed around for them to bring home. The design is finalized and we have contacted the factory into making it. For our next round of local events, we can apply them directly.

CLICK ⬆️ to check our video please!

Specific missions or a broader story? Both. Each relic has its own Dossier card: when and where it landed, what it did, how it came to rest, and the team behind it. Placed around a loop from Earth Base to the Moon, Mars and deep space, the relics together tell the broader story of NASA exploration from the 1960s to the 2020s, and how much these machines gave to science before they were forgotten.

Which perspectives do we highlight? Three. The relics themselves, through each one's Burial Mystery of how it came to rest. The people behind each mission, named on every card and honored in Crew Roles inspired by real astronauts. And the players, as future explorers in the year 2069 who protect each site where it rests and share what they learn.

The main idea we want players to leave with

Equipment left on other worlds isn't junk. Each relic is a piece of history with a story: what it is, how it came to rest, who made it happen, and what it taught us. We want players to leave knowing that these sites deserve to be protected where they rest, and that knowledge grows when it is shared.

Development and prototype

Our first idea was a 3D rover-driving game with Earth, Moon and Mars stages. Building it from scratch in a game engine was more than our time and resources allowed. We kept the rover and turned it into Exploration, a 2D web game where players drive SCOUT.

Our first board game borrowed from classic board games, with relics bought and rented like property. We also tried a sliding-tile maze and a Top Trumps-style card game before coming back to the board. Then we changed the core idea: these relics are history, not property. We replaced buying and renting with an expedition team that discovers each relic, learns how it came to rest, and restores its site.

We wrote the rules as the Expedition Field Manual, modeled on classic board-game rulebooks, so it also works as the storytelling guide. It includes a Relic Archive with each relic's story and a Detective's Notebook of clues. The online board game follows the same rules, so players can move between the table and the screen.
